title: Telus picks up pace on sale of health, agriculture and VC divisions
byline: Andrew Willis; Irene Galea; Clare O’Hara
html:
This summer, Telus chief executive officer Victor Dodig launched a back-to-basics strategy that included potential asset sales that could raise more than $4-billion.Cole Burston/The Globe and Mail

Telus Corp. T-T is breaking down its health, agriculture and venture capital businesses into bite-sized morsels for potential buyers as the telecom attempts to speed up a transformation plan after fielding an unexpected takeover proposal from rival Quebecor Inc. QBR-A-T

This summer, Telus chief executive officer Victor Dodig launched a back-to-basics strategy at the Vancouver-based telecom that included potential asset sales that could raise more than $4-billion. Last week, on the day Quebecor revealed an audacious $31-billion takeover proposal, Mr. Dodig said in an interview the company has embraced “an acceleration of our monetization of our non-core telecom assets.”

Potential buyers such as insurance companies are hoping to take advantage of Mr. Dodig’s need for speed by making offers at prices lower than what they would have paid before Quebecor went public with its proposal, according to two sources familiar with the process.

The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources because they are not permitted to speak for the companies.

Mr. Dodig plans to use the cash from asset sales to pay down debt and invest in telecom growth opportunities such as infrastructure for data centres. The asset sales also have a symbolic importance, demonstrating that the new CEO can meet performance targets he set this summer.

The most likely buyers of the Telus Health divisions are domestic life insurers that offer benefits to company employees. The insurers are interested in acquiring Telus units that fit neatly into regions or business lines where they already have operations, including benefit plans for large Canadian companies, the two sources said. The insurers don’t want to pay for Telus businesses in the U.S. and other countries where they don’t operate.

The continuing divestiture process has revealed Telus Health is is not worth what the company previously pegged its value at. In its second quarter, Telus took an $800-million non-cash impairment charge on its health business. In a recent report, analyst Drew McReynolds at RBC Capital Markets said the enterprise value of Telus Health – its debt plus its equity – is about $3-billion.

Telus is pulling apart a health, agriculture and VC portfolio built over two decades through numerous acquisitions. Notable purchases include its $2.3-billion acquisition of Lifeworks in 2022 and of Workplace Options for $500-million in 2025.

The strategy under former CEO Darren Entwistle was to find efficiencies between the companies, and build an entity that could stand alone from Telus, possibly through a spinoff, as the company did with Telus International, its phone centre arm.

In 2021, the telecom sold a portion of Telus International through a $1.36-billion initial public offering. In the fall of 2025, Telus bought back the public stake in the company, now known as Telus Digital, after the spinoff’s share price fell more than 90 per cent over four years.

While the company found some synergies between the health group’s divisions, Telus faced challenges uniting the businesses it had acquired into an effective whole, according to two additional sources. At times, the company’s different divisions were competing for the same projects, and Telus Health saw rapid changes in leadership, one of the sources told The Globe.

Mr. Dodig, shown in Toronto last week, plans to use the cash from asset sales to pay down debt and invest in growth opportunities.Fred Lum/The Globe and Mail

Telus has faced a long road in its attempts to sell the division. In January, the company hired TD Securities Inc. and Jefferies Securities Inc. to run the process.

Initially, Telus focused on finding a private equity or sovereign wealth fund that would buy a minority stake in Telus Health and set a premium value on the entire business. In March, Telus executives said they hoped to have a prospective partner in place before Mr. Dodig succeeded Mr. Entwistle in July.

However, the company was not able to secure a deal, in part because many buyers were only interested in certain segments of the platform. When Mr. Dodig took on the role, the strategy changed.

At a conference in September, Mr. Dodig described a division made of three parts, which the company was marketing separately: a retirement benefit and pension consulting service, an employee-benefit business connected to the government health system and the workplace health business that includes the Lifeworks business.

“I’m pretty confident that two of those, maybe three, over time will be in the hands of other owners,” he said at the time.

In early November, Mr. Dodig said the company is in “advanced discussions” to divest of one of the three portions of the health business, and to bring another to market within the month.

Mr. Dodig also put a “For Sale” sign on Telus Global Ventures, a collection of investments in 160 companies. Last year, Telus valued the portfolio at $930-million. The company launched the business in 2001.

“We’re going to be reviewing our Telus Ventures portfolio,” Mr. Dodig said in an analyst call in August. “Everything is really on the table in terms of understanding our portfolio, understanding those things we’d like to keep and also ensuring that there’s a monetization program in place.”

Telus has hired BMO Capital Markets to oversee the sales process of some of the businesses at Telus Ventures, according to two sources. Last year, the division raised $45-mllion from selling what Telus described as “non-strategic investments” and posted a $72-million profit.

With a report from Sean Silcoff
summary: Telecom accelerates plan to divest of non-core assets after fielding Quebecor’s takeover proposal
